chunks: And by this chain, from Badr -the slave of Ahmad ibn al-Hasan- who said:

I arrived at the mountain region, and at that time I did not affirm the Imamate, but I loved them generally. Then Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik died, and he bequeathed to me in his illness that the Shahri Simand (horse), his sword, and his belt be delivered to his master. I feared that if I did not deliver the Shahri to Idhkutakain, he would subject me to humiliation. So I valued the beast, the sword, and the belt at seven hundred dinars for myself, and did not inform anyone of this. Then a letter arrived from Iraq ordering me: 'Send the seven hundred dinars that are ours from before you, from the price of the Shahri Simand, the sword, and the belt.'

key_terms.الشَّهْرِيُّ السِّمَنْدُ: Shahri Simand, a specific breed of horse
key_terms.الْعِرَاقِ: Iraq, the region from which the letter arrived
key_terms.بَدْرٌ: Badr, a slave of Ahmad ibn Hasan
key_terms.يَزِيدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ: Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik, the Umayyad Caliph

ai.seo_question: What is the story of Badr and the seven hundred dinars in Kitab al-Ghayba?
ai.summary: This narrative from *Kitab al-Ghayba* highlights the practical reality of the Imam's hidden wealth and administrative network during the Minor Occultation, illustrating how agents like Badr managed assets with precision to avoid political scrutiny. The story underscores the continuity of the Imamate's economic authority, as the specific valuation of the horse, sword, and belt was pre-arranged and confirmed by correspondence from Iraq, demonstrating the organized infrastructure supporting the Imam's occultation.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: H 241 - It is narrated from the same chains from Badr, the slave of Ahmad Ibn Hasan, from his father that he said:

“I arrived at the mountain region. In those days I was not a believer in Imamate, but loved them over all. Until, Yazid Ibn Abdul Malik died and he bequeathed in his malady that Shahriul Samand (a breed of horse), his sword and his belt should be given to his lord. I was afraid if I did not give Shahriul Samand to Idhkutakain, he would chastise me. I valued the beast, sword and the belt for seven hundred dinars and took them on my account and did not tell anyone. Then a letter came from Iraq ordering me, “Send the seven hundred dinars that you owe us for the price of Shahriul­ Samand, the sword and the belt.”
